description:
KInference — the inference control plane's own view of itself: pick outcomes, routing policy, prefix-cache affinity and the health of the signals those decisions depend on.

SCOPE. Everything here is fleet-level. /metrics carries no per-worker label anywhere, so the per-worker table and the prefix overlap map from the built-in SPA on :9001 have no equivalent and are not reproduced. Engine-side KV pressure and queue depth are vllm:* / sglang:* series scraped from the workers, not re-exported by kinference — those live on the vLLM dashboards linked in the dropdown above, which open time-synced.

READING IT. Every *Vec family is absent until its first observation, so an empty panel usually means 'has not happened yet' rather than zero. Only kinference_build_info and kinference_leader exist from startup; alert on those, never on series absence.

links.title: vLLM / SGLang workers
links.tooltip: Engine-side KV pressure and queue depth

panels.title: Health
panels.description: Top-line health of KInference itself. Everything here is fleet-wide; per-worker drill-down lives in the built-in SPA on :9001, because /metrics carries no per-worker label anywhere.

panels.title: Leader
panels.description: `kinference_leader` is 1 on the replica holding the Lease. SUMMED, not maxed — the whole point is to tell 0 (no leader, discovery stalled) from 2 (split brain). `max()` reports 1 for both of those and for the healthy case.

panels.title: Success rate
panels.description:
Share of `Pick()` calls returning `ok`. Deliberately NOT clamped: at zero traffic this shows 'idle' rather than a synthetic 100%, because a fake success rate is indistinguishable from a real one. Thresholds are PLACEHOLDERS — the code supplies none. Recalibrate from your own baseline.

Read it against the outcome graph below: a dip is either `no_workers` (discovery or readiness) or `bad_request` (the caller), and those need different people.

panels.title: Prefix match ratio
panels.description: Layered prefix overlap as a share of blocks requested — radix-tree hits plus in-flight prefill credit. NO tenant selector: the prefix families carry `model` and `qos` only, and adding `tenant=~"$tenant"` silently returns empty. Can legitimately exceed 100% under DP>1 double-publish, so the axis is uncapped. Thresholds are PLACEHOLDERS.

panels.title: Request p95
panels.description: End-to-end p95 from `kinference_request_duration_ms` — pick to final token. The only latency family spanning BOTH local and provider picks, and the only one that sees non-streaming requests. Buckets top out at 600000 ms; once more than ~1% of samples land in `+Inf` this number is fiction.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_request_duration_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Worker fleet
panels.description:
Fleet reachability over time, split by served model and STACKED, so the top of the stack is the total worker count and each band is one model's contribution.

Stacking is meaningful here and mostly is not elsewhere on this dashboard: these series are disjoint counts of the same thing, so their sum is a real quantity. Caveat inherent to it — a series sitting at zero still draws its line at the current top of the stack, so with `unresponsive` normally at 0 you will see its line riding along the top of the `ok` bands. That is the stack working, not a fault.

FROM `kinference_workers_by_model`, NOT `kinference_workers`. The two are separate families on purpose: a worker serving several models (LoRA adapters) is counted under EACH model here, so the stack total can EXCEED the fleet size in that case. `kinference_workers{state}` remains the authoritative total — reach for that, not for the top of this stack.

MAXED across replicas, not summed: every kinference replica observes the same fleet, so summing multiplies it by the replica count. `unresponsive` means the last successful scrape is older than 5000 ms, a threshold that lives in the metric itself (`derive_health` in telemetry.rs) and is shared with the built-in SPA so the two surfaces cannot disagree. Such workers are still routable; this is staleness, not removal. A model whose worker set is deleted drops to zero rather than freezing at its last count.

panels.title: Responses
panels.description: Every `Pick()` by wire outcome. `no_workers` means discovery or readiness, not policy — cross-check against the worker graph on the left. Distinct from `kinference_policy_decisions_total` in the Routing row: a pick that resolved no policy at all still returns `ok`, so the two can disagree without either being wrong.

panels.title: Decision latency
panels.description: How long kinference itself took to answer `Pick()`. This is NOT model latency — it is tokenize + prefix lookup + scoring + policy. Filtered to `outcome="ok"` on purpose: `no_workers` picks fail fast and, left in, drag the aggregate p99 DOWN exactly when the fleet is broken. Buckets top out at 5000 ms.

panels.title: Degraded responses
panels.description: Share of successful picks that fell back to load-only scoring because tokenize or the prefix index was unavailable. This is kinference's characteristic silent failure: still routing, no longer routing WELL. Every other panel in this row stays green while this rises. The `on() group_left()` is mandatory — the numerator carries a `reason` label the denominator lacks, and a bare `/` returns an empty vector with no error.

panels.title: Memory usage
panels.description:
Container working set per kinference pod, against its configured limit. NOT a kinference metric: the registry is a fresh `Registry::new()` rather than the default one, so there are no `process_*` collectors and this comes from cAdvisor and kube-state-metrics instead.

Worth a panel because kinference's memory is dominated by things that grow with traffic rather than with time: the radix prefix index and the request-body buffer. Working set climbing toward the limit while `kinference_index_blocks` climbs too is the index; climbing while `kinference_body_buffer_bytes` climbs is a body leak.

panels.title: CPU usage
panels.description:
Container CPU per kinference pod against its limit, in cores. Like the memory panel beside it this comes from cAdvisor and kube-state-metrics, not from kinference — the registry is a fresh `Registry::new()` so there are no `process_*` collectors.

THE SERIES TO WATCH IS `throttled` ON THE RIGHT AXIS, not the cores line. CFS enforces a CPU limit per 100ms period, so a container at half its limit on average can still be stalled inside individual periods — and a picker being stalled shows up to callers as `Pick()` latency, not as high CPU. Cores can look comfortable while throttling is hurting; if `throttled` is persistently non-zero, raise the limit rather than reading the average as reassurance.

Cross-read with the decision-latency panel above: throttling and a p99 rise together mean the limit, not the workload.

panels.title: Worker evictions
panels.description:
Cumulative workers kinference evicted ITSELF, since this process started — the raw counter, not a rate, so the line only ever steps up and a drop to zero means kinference restarted.

An eviction is not a pod going away. A pod that simply disappears arrives as a discovery removal, is logged "worker removed" at INFO, and is deliberately NOT counted here — otherwise every rolling restart would read as a fault. This counts only the cases where the worker was discovered and healthy but disagreed with its pool about something the pool cannot vary per worker, so it had to be dropped to keep the rest serving on coherent assumptions.

ANY NON-ZERO VALUE IS A CONFIG MISMATCH, not a transient. `block_size_mismatch` means the engine publishes a different tokens-per-block than the worker set's `kvBlockSize` — kinference waits for three consecutive mismatched events before acting, so this is not a bad frame. `model_mismatch` means the worker's /v1/models disagrees with the pool's canonical set.

The eviction is silent in every other panel: the worker vanishes from `kinference_workers` and the fleet just looks smaller. The WARN log carries both mismatched values and names the fix.

panels.title: Token overview
panels.description: Token volume and request shape across the fleet: prefill and decode by QoS and model, what the engine served from its own cache, and whether the reports these are built from could be attributed at all. Per-tenant breakdowns live in the row below.

panels.title: Token throughput
panels.description: Tokens per second from terminal reports. `cached prompt` is what the ENGINE said it served from its own prefix cache (proto `cached_tokens`), which is a different quantity from kinference's own prefix match ratio in the Prefix cache row — they are deliberately kept in separate rows so nobody puts them on one axis.

panels.title: Prompt tokens
panels.description:
Prefill volume split by QoS class and served model — the input side of the pair, read against the completion panel to its right. The two scale different costs: prefill grows with the prompt, decode with the completion, and a model heavy on one occupies GPU quite differently from a model heavy on the other.

Includes prompt tokens the ENGINE served from its own KV cache, which cost no prefill compute. Subtract `kinference_cached_prompt_tokens_total` — the `cached prompt` series on the throughput panel to the left — for the tokens that actually did work.

Carries the same orphan distortion as the completion panel: a report whose `response_id` kinference could not resolve lands under `qos="unknown"`, not under the class it was picked with. See the orphaned-reports panel below.

targets.expr: sum by (qos, model) (rate(kinference_prompt_tokens_total{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Completion tokens
panels.description:
Decode volume split by QoS class and served model: which models are generating, and under which service class. Read against the prompt side of the throughput panel to the left — prefill scales with the prompt, decode with the completion, and a model heavy here is occupying GPU differently from one heavy there.

ONE DISTORTION TO KNOW ABOUT. When a `response_id` is unknown or its labels aged out of the 600s TTL, `report_final_token` has nothing to attribute the report to and falls back to `qos="interactive"` (and the default tenant). So the `interactive` series silently absorbs every orphaned report, whatever class it was actually picked under. If it looks implausibly large, compare the pick rate against the attributed-report rate before concluding anything about your QoS mix.

All four pickers apply, `$tenant` included — this is the whole fleet only while the tenant picker is on All.

targets.expr: sum by (qos, model) (rate(kinference_completion_tokens_total{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Engine-reported prefix reuse
panels.description: `cached_tokens / prompt_tokens` — the engine's own account of how much of each prompt it served from its KV cache. Split by model. Systematically undercounted whenever a backend omits the field, so read it next to the panel on its right — and a model that has never reported the field has NO line here rather than a zero one, because the numerator series does not exist.

targets.expr:
sum by (model) (rate(kinference_cached_prompt_tokens_total{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))
/
sum by (model) (rate(kinference_prompt_tokens_total{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Request shape
panels.description: Token-count distribution per request. Buckets are EXPONENTIAL (8 → 262144), and `histogram_quantile` interpolates linearly inside a bucket, so every quantile is biased high within its own bucket. Read these as order-of-magnitude; do not quote a p95 prompt length to four significant figures.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_prompt_length_tokens_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_prompt_length_tokens_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_completion_length_tokens_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_completion_length_tokens_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Orphaned reports
panels.description:
Final-token reports whose `response_id` kinference never issued, or whose labels aged out of the 600s TTL. Nothing is left to attribute them to, so THREE labels are wrong at once: `model` falls back to the caller's own request field rather than the resolved pick — which can put an ALIAS into the model label that appears nowhere else — `tenant` drops to the default bucket, and `qos` is reported as `unknown` rather than being guessed.

So this is not just a lost row: it is that many rows of every per-request family misattributed. A steady non-zero means the caller is holding response_ids past the TTL; a spike usually means kinference restarted with requests in flight, which orphans every one of them.

A DIRECT counter, not a derived one. The same fact is visible as `prompt_length_tokens_count - request_duration_ms_count`, since the duration is the one family skipped for an orphan — but that is a difference between counters aggregated over different label sets, which is exactly the shape that made the cached-tokens ratio read 200%.

panels.title: Per-tenant overview
panels.description: Everything kinference records per tenant, in one place. These ten families are the only ones carrying a `tenant` label; prefix-cache metrics and `kinference_provider_ttft_ms` do not.

panels.title: Requests by tenant: local or provider
panels.description:
Where each tenant's requests went: kept on the cluster (`Local`, a worker set) or sent off it (`Provider`).

Use this rather than reading the split off the token panels: their `model` is the model each request was sent with (the worker's, or the provider row's `name`), and a model name alone does not say where it ran.

One count per pick that chose a destination, so it says where requests were SENT, whether or not they then succeeded; a caller that retries starts over with a fresh pick and counts again. A pick that routed nothing (no workers, a policy rejection) is not here. The model and QoS pickers do not apply: this family carries neither label.

panels.title: Requests by tenant and destination
panels.description:
The same picks by destination: the worker set or provider, by the name a policy uses for it (`backend.name`). Series count is tenants × destinations.

One count per pick that chose a destination, so it says where requests were SENT, whether or not they then succeeded; a caller that retries starts over with a fresh pick and counts again. A pick that routed nothing (no workers, a policy rejection) is not here. The model and QoS pickers do not apply: this family carries neither label.

panels.title: Share of requests sent to providers
panels.description:
The fraction of each tenant's picks that went off-cluster: 0 means all of it stayed local, 1 means none did. A tenant with traffic but no provider picks reads 0 rather than dropping out of the chart.

One count per pick that chose a destination, so it says where requests were SENT, whether or not they then succeeded; a caller that retries starts over with a fresh pick and counts again. A pick that routed nothing (no workers, a policy rejection) is not here. The model and QoS pickers do not apply: this family carries neither label.

targets.expr: (sum by (tenant) (rate(kinference_routed_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", tenant=~"$tenant", type="Provider"}[$__rate_interval])) or 0 * sum by (tenant) (rate(kinference_routed_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))) / sum by (tenant) (rate(kinference_routed_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: E2E p95
panels.description: The trend behind the table's `E2E p95` column, and the one latency series with no population gap: it covers local and provider picks, streaming and non-streaming alike.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tenant) (rate(kinference_request_duration_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: TTFT p95
panels.description: Local AND streaming only. A tenant missing here but present in the E2E panel is not broken — it is either routed to a provider or not streaming. Compare against the TTFT coverage panel in the Latency row before concluding anything from a gap.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tenant) (rate(kinference_ttft_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: ITL p95
panels.description: Inter-token latency by tenant. `kinference_itl_ms_bucket` is an IntCounterVec whose name already ends in `_bucket` — never let a query builder append another. Empty for any tenant whose responses carry fewer than two chunks.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tenant) (rate(kinference_itl_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Prompt length p95
panels.description:
Request SHAPE rather than performance: how large a prompt each tenant sends. Useful for spotting the tenant whose prefill cost dominates the fleet, and for reading the latency panels above — a tenant with a high E2E p95 and a high prompt p95 is expensive, not necessarily badly served.

Buckets are EXPONENTIAL (8 → 262144) and `histogram_quantile` interpolates linearly inside a bucket, so every value here is biased high within its own bucket. Read it as an order of magnitude; the log axis is a reminder of that, not a stylistic choice.

Unlike the TTFT and ITL panels above, this has NO population gap: it is recorded for every terminal report regardless of streaming or backend.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tenant) (rate(kinference_prompt_length_tokens_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Completion length p95
panels.description:
How much each tenant generates. Paired with the prompt panel beside it this separates the two costs that a single latency number conflates: prefill scales with the prompt, decode scales with the completion.

Same exponential-bucket caveat as the prompt panel — order of magnitude, not a precise token count. Also recorded for every terminal report, so no population gap.

A tenant high here and low on prompt length is a decode-bound workload, and the one whose ITL p95 matters most.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tenant) (rate(kinference_completion_length_tokens_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Prompt tokens
panels.description:
Prefill volume per (tenant, model) pair. Splitting by BOTH is what makes this answer a question neither label answers alone: not just who is expensive, but which model they are expensive ON. A tenant spread across two models is two different cost profiles that a tenant-only line averages into one.

Paired with the completion panel below rather than summed into a single 'tokens' series, for the same reason the two length panels above are separate — prefill and decode are different costs. Heavy here means expensive to admit; heavy below means expensive to finish.

Counts tokens the engine may have served from its own KV cache, so this is admitted volume rather than compute performed. `kinference_cached_prompt_tokens_total` carries both labels too if you need the difference.

Series count is tenants × models, and `metrics.tenant_labels = "all"` leaves the tenant side unbounded — use the pickers rather than reading a crowded chart.

targets.expr: sum by (tenant, model) (rate(kinference_prompt_tokens_total{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Completion tokens
panels.description:
Decode volume per tenant — the closest thing here to a billing-shaped number, and the one to treat most carefully.

NOT BILLING-GRADE, for three reasons the panel cannot show. `tenant="default"` is a reserved mixing bucket (unattributed requests, tenants off the allowlist, callers literally sending `default`). Orphaned reports land in it too, whatever tenant they really belonged to. And the whole label is only meaningful while `metrics.tenant_labels` is set — under the DEFAULT `none` policy every series collapses into that one bucket.

Check the orphaned-reports panel in the Token overview row before quoting any of this at someone.

targets.expr: sum by (tenant, model) (rate(kinference_completion_tokens_total{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Uncached prompt tokens
panels.description:
Prompt tokens per (tenant, model) that actually cost prefill compute: total prompt tokens minus the ones the ENGINE reports it served from its own KV cache. The panel above counts volume ADMITTED; this one counts work DONE, and the gap between them is what prefix-cache routing is buying you.

This is the closest thing on the dashboard to per-tenant GPU cost. Read it rather than the prompt-token panel when apportioning: a tenant sending huge but highly repetitive prompts is cheap here and expensive above.

THE `or ... * 0` IS LOAD-BEARING, not defensive noise. `cached_prompt_tokens` is only incremented when a report actually carries `cached_tokens`; `prompt_tokens` is incremented either way. So a (tenant, model) that has never had the field reported has no cached series at all — and PromQL binary operators DROP unmatched series silently, which would make that pair vanish from this chart rather than show its full uncached total. The `or` substitutes a zero so the subtraction still matches.

targets.expr:
sum by (tenant, model) (rate(kinference_prompt_tokens_total{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))
-
(
  sum by (tenant, model) (rate(kinference_cached_prompt_tokens_total{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))
  or
  sum by (tenant, model) (rate(kinference_prompt_tokens_total{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])) * 0
)

panels.title: Latency
panels.description: End-to-end, TTFT, ITL and provider latency. Read the end-to-end panel first — it is the only one with no population gaps.

panels.title: End-to-end duration
panels.description: Pick to final token, from `kinference_request_duration_ms`. THE ONE HONEST CROSS-POPULATION LATENCY NUMBER on this dashboard: the only family covering local AND provider picks, streaming AND non-streaming. Excludes reports whose `response_id` was unknown or TTL-swept, since those carry no `picked_at` to measure from.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_request_duration_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_request_duration_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_request_duration_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: End-to-end p95
panels.description: Same family, split by model. Bucket saturation check: `sum(rate(kinference_request_duration_ms_bucket{le="+Inf"}[5m])) - sum(rate(kinference_request_duration_ms_bucket{le="600000"}[5m]))` — once that is non-trivial, the p95 has hit the top of the ladder and is no longer meaningful.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, model) (rate(kinference_request_duration_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: TTFT
panels.description: Time to first token. TWO EXCLUSIONS, both silent. (1) Local picks only — provider picks are in `kinference_provider_ttft_ms` instead. (2) Streaming only — `finalize_observation` returns early for a non-streaming pick before reaching `record_ttft`, because there the 'first token' arrives at completion and the figure would be total latency wearing a TTFT label. A tenant that is 100% provider-routed or 100% non-streaming shows EMPTY here, which reads as 'no traffic'. The coverage panel below turns that caveat into a number.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_ttft_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_ttft_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_ttft_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: TTFT coverage
panels.description: `ttft_ms_count / request_duration_ms_count`. The antidote to the panel above: `1 - this` is your combined provider + non-streaming share. If this sits well below 1 and you are trying to use TTFT as a saturation signal, it is telling you the signal is blind to most of your traffic.

targets.expr:
sum(rate(kinference_ttft_ms_count{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))
/
sum(rate(kinference_request_duration_ms_count{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Inter-token latency
panels.description:
THE SUBTLEST QUERY HERE. `kinference_itl_ms_bucket` is an IntCounterVec whose NAME ALREADY ENDS IN `_bucket` — Grafana's histogram query builder auto-appends the suffix and produces `kinference_itl_ms_bucket_bucket`, which matches nothing and errors nowhere. Hand-write this query. There is also NO `kinference_itl_ms_sum`, so no mean or average is derivable for ITL anywhere, ever.

The `gaps/s` series on the right axis is `kinference_itl_ms_count`, which equals the `+Inf` bucket. Read the quantiles against it: a p99 over a handful of samples is noise. It is also the ITL coverage signal — the proto prescribes an EMPTY bucket vector for any response with fewer than two chunks, so every non-streaming request and every single-chunk stream contributes nothing here. If this sits far below your request rate, ITL is blind to most of your traffic.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_itl_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_itl_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(kinference_itl_ms_bucket{namespace="$namespace", model=~"$model", qos=~"$qos", tenant=~"$tenant"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Provider TTFT
panels.description: Off-cluster picks only. This family carries `provider` and `model` and NOTHING ELSE — applying $qos or $tenant returns empty, so the standard selector block is edited here rather than copy-pasted. Also success-and-streaming only: a 401 or 5xx carries a time-to-ERROR, and folding that in would make a failing vendor look fast.

panels.title: End-to-end duration
panels.description: The 16 explicit buckets of `kinference_request_duration_ms` shown as a distribution rather than as quantiles. Worth its width: this traffic is bimodal (short chats vs long generations) and a p50 lands in the empty middle where no real request lives.

panels.title: Routing & policy
panels.description: How the InferencePolicy CRD resolved picks, which rules fired, and whether worker sets were admitted.

panels.title: Policy decisions
panels.description: How the InferencePolicy CRD resolved each pick. Nine outcomes. `unmatched_served` is a FAIL-OPEN, not an error — no rule matched and the request was served anyway. `rejected_on_empty` is distinct from `unmatched_empty`: the first means a rule matched but every candidate was excluded under `onEmpty: Reject`; the second means no rule matched at all.

panels.title: Policy rule matches
panels.description: Which `InferencePolicy` rules actually fire. `rule` is a free-form operator-authored string with no cardinality bound, so the `topk` is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Series will flap in and out of the legend across a range query — that is `topk` behaving normally, not a data problem. A rule that never appears here is either unreachable or shadowed by an earlier one.

panels.title: Policy rejection ratio
panels.description: Written as an ALLOWLIST of good outcomes rather than a denylist of bad ones, for two reasons. First, `unmatched_served` is a fail-open — the obvious `outcome!="chosen"` counts fail-opens as failures and pages you during normal operation. Second, a future tenth outcome then defaults to 'counted as a problem' rather than silently landing in the healthy bucket.

panels.title: Fail-open
panels.description: Its own panel because 'policy is not being enforced, but nothing is failing' is a distinct operational state that the rejection ratio deliberately excludes. A sustained non-zero here usually means a policyRef is missing or a CRD failed to compile.

panels.title: Policy revision mismatch
panels.description: Picks naming a pool revision this replica does not hold — a caller and the control plane disagreeing about the current InferencePool generation. Any non-zero is worth a look; sustained non-zero means a stale client or a reconcile that never landed.

panels.title: Leader election
panels.description: Lease churn. Steady transitions mean the Lease is flapping between replicas, which restarts discovery and resets the prefix index each time. `election errors` are failed Lease reads/writes against the apiserver.

panels.title: Worker-set admission rejections
panels.description: `InferenceWorkerSet`s that produced no pool. A bar gauge over $__range rather than a rate timeseries, because these fire at reconcile time in bursts and a per-second rate of a config error is not a meaningful quantity. NOTE the reason values are CamelCase (`MissingProfile`, `KvEventsMissingPort`) — unlike every other reason label in the system, which is snake_case. A snake_case filter here matches nothing and renders as 'no config errors'. `increase()` extrapolates, so a single event can render as 1.06; decimals are pinned to 0.

panels.title: Prefix cache
panels.description: How much of each prompt the picker found already cached. These families carry `model` and `qos` only — no `tenant`.

panels.title: Prefix match ratio
panels.description: TWO NUMERATORS OVER ONE DENOMINATOR. `matched` is the layered overlap the picker actually scored on (radix tree plus credit for prefill already in flight); `radix_matched` is the raw tree hit for the same picks. THE GAP BETWEEN THE LINES IS THE IN-FLIGHT PREFILL CREDIT — that is the reason for plotting both. The axis is deliberately uncapped: layered can legitimately exceed 1.0 under DP>1 double-publish, and clamping would hide the very anomaly the overmatch panel counts. Degraded picks are excluded from these counters.

panels.title: Prefix match ratio
panels.description: A heatmap rather than quantiles because this distribution is bimodal by nature — cold picks at 0, warm picks near 1 — and a p50 lands in the empty middle where no real pick lives. The family has an explicit `le="0"` bucket, so a genuine zero-overlap pick is countable separately from the 0–10% band; do not collapse the bottom bin.

panels.title: Cold-start picks
panels.description:
Share of picks that matched NOTHING. This panel is only possible because the family carries an explicit lowest bucket at 0.0 — without it the nearest query is `le="0.1"`, which means 'matched at most 10%', a materially different and much larger number.

The bucket edge renders as `le="0.0"`, WITH the decimal — that is how the Rust prometheus crate formats an f64 bound, and `le="0"` matches nothing. Exact match rather than a regex on purpose: PromQL string literals use Go escaping, so `\.` inside a double-quoted selector is a parse error, not an escaped dot.

panels.title: Prefix overmatch
panels.description: Picks where matched blocks exceeded requested blocks — the DP>1 double-publish signature. Deliberately NOT normalised against `prefix_requested_blocks_total`: overmatch counts PICKS, requested counts BLOCKS, and the ratio is dimensionally meaningless while looking like a small reassuring number.

panels.title: Prefix blocks
panels.description: Volume context for the ratio panels. A 90% match ratio over 3 blocks/s is not the same fact as 90% over 30k blocks/s, and the ratio alone cannot tell you which you are looking at.

panels.title: Prefix index health
panels.description: Whether the radix tree that cache-affinity routing depends on is actually being fed. Gauges here refresh on a throttled ~10s dump.

panels.title: Indexed blocks
panels.description: Blocks in the radix tree. Shown PER REPLICA rather than aggregated, because each replica maintains its own index and divergence between them is itself the bug. NOTE this gauge refreshes on a throttled ~10s tree dump, NOT per scrape — do not apply `deriv()` or `delta()` over short windows, and do not alert on short-window change. The stair-steps are a dump-cadence artifact.

panels.title: Index coverage
panels.description: What fraction of reachable workers are actually publishing KV events. Sustained below 1 means cache-affinity routing is blind to some workers while every other panel looks healthy. The `on (pod)` is mandatory — the right-hand side carries an extra `state` label and a bare `/` returns empty. The two gauges also update on different cadences (index ~10s throttled, workers per scrape), so the ratio transiently over- and undershoots 1; only sustained deviation is real.

panels.title: Index events
panels.description: KV-cache events applied to the radix tree. `cleared` is the one to watch: a spike means a worker dropped its whole KV view and its cache affinity resets to cold, which shows up minutes later as a dip in the prefix match ratio.

panels.title: Index churn
panels.description: Net (stored − removed) should track the slope of the indexed-blocks gauge above. A persistent divergence between the two means the throttled gauge and the per-event counters disagree, which is worth knowing about on its own.

panels.title: Tokenization
panels.description: Which tokenizer served each request, how fast, and whether the local tokenizer agrees with the engine. A divergence here breaks prefix routing silently.

panels.title: Tokenization paths
panels.description:
How each request got tokenized, in requests per minute — exactly one attempt per request, so the three lines sum to the tokenize rate.

Absolute rates rather than a percentage share: a percent-stacked view normalises away the thing you actually want to know. At low volume one fallback out of two attempts reads as a terrifying 50%, and at high volume a real regression can look like a small slice.

`unavailable` should move in lockstep with the `tokenize` series in the degraded-responses panel on the Health row; if it does not, something else is degrading scoring.

panels.title: Tokenize duration
panels.description: This family has NO LABELS. `local` and `http_fallback` latency are not separable here, and $model returns empty. The p99 is dominated by whichever path is currently hot, so read it beside the path mix on the left or not at all.

panels.title: Tokenizer compare
panels.description: THE MOST MISLEADING ZERO ON THIS DASHBOARD. These counters are only ever non-zero in compare mode, so `0 divergence` is NOT evidence of agreement — it almost always means compare mode is off. When divergence IS non-zero, every prefix block hash is wrong, cache-affinity routing has silently stopped working, and every panel except the prefix match ratio will still look healthy.

defaults.noValue: compare mode not enabled — this panel proves nothing

panels.title: Admission control & body store
panels.description: The request-body buffer.

panels.title: Body buffer
panels.description: Request bodies currently held for the pull-based body flow. PER REPLICA, never summed: the body store is per-process and one hot replica is exactly the failure mode a fleet sum erases. Reported in BYTES, while the config knob that bounds it (`body_max_total_kb`) is in KB.

panels.title: Body store
panels.description: `pushed − reaped` sustained above zero is the leak rate driving the buffer panel upward. Bodies are reclaimed by a TTL sweep, so a healthy system has these two tracking each other with a lag equal to the TTL.

panels.title: Body rejections
panels.description: `server_full` is a CAPACITY signal needing operator action; `declared_too_large`, `request_too_large` and `chunk_too_large` are CLIENT errors needing none. Different meanings in one family — never alert on their sum.

panels.title: Body aborts
panels.description: `backend_unauthorized` and `backend_unresolved` are routing or config bugs. `not_dispatched` is the normal outcome for a client that changed its mind and is not a fault at all. `pull_failed` is a backend problem. Same family, three different meanings — the colour split is what makes this readable.

panels.title: KV cache usage
panels.description:
The value an `InferencePolicy` `drop: {kvCacheUsage: ...}` clause compares against: KV-cache utilization per worker, averaged over 30s.

This is the EXACT value the predicate reads, not an approximation of it — so a threshold read off this graph is a threshold that will behave as drawn.

THE HEADROOM SIGNAL, and the one to prefer for "this GPU is full". It rises monotonically with pressure, which the queue does not: measured on this fleet, a moment at 93% KV carried one queued prompt while a moment at 31% carried five — so a queue threshold ranks those two backwards.

The red line at 0.9 is the threshold `inferencepolicy-3` and `-4` ship with. Watch where your fleet actually sits before trusting it.

Published once per (worker, model) because the value is joinable against the per-model families, but it is a property of the ENGINE — so this collapses the duplicate model rows with `max by (worker)`. The `$model` variable still filters which workers appear.

panels.title: Queued prompts
panels.description:
The value an `InferencePolicy` `drop: {queuedPrompts: ...}` clause compares against: `num_requests_waiting` per worker, averaged over 30s.

This is the EXACT value the predicate reads, not an approximation of it — so a threshold read off this graph is a threshold that will behave as drawn.

FRACTIONAL, because it is a mean. A worker that queued 5 prompts for two seconds out of thirty reads about 0.3; one genuinely backed up across the window reads near 5. That is the whole reason for the window — the raw gauge is bursty under continuous batching, spiking for seconds and clearing, so a threshold on the instantaneous value sheds load over a transient that has already passed.

It follows that `greaterThan: 0` is far stricter than it looks: it fires on any queueing at all in the window. A fractional bound is usually what an interactive rule wants.

Published once per (worker, model) because the value is joinable against the per-model families, but it is a property of the ENGINE — so this collapses the duplicate model rows with `max by (worker)`. The `$model` variable still filters which workers appear.

panels.title: Predicted TTFT p95
panels.description:
The value an `InferencePolicy` `drop: {predictedTTFT: ...}` clause compares against, at p95. Observed for EVERY candidate the engine scored, not just the winner — a threshold applies to every candidate too, and the winner's distribution is biased low precisely because it won.

p95 ACROSS WORKERS, not per worker. `histogram_quantile` needs enough observations in the window to mean anything, and one worker's share of a low-traffic minute often is not enough; the aggregate stays honest. The `worker` label is on the metric, so `sum by (le, worker)` splits it out once traffic supports that.

Buckets are deliberately `kinference_ttft_ms`'s, so this reads directly against the OBSERVED p95 in the Latency section — "predicted 2s, delivered 5s" is the calibration question, and it is also how you catch a stale profile fit.

Recorded whether or not a policy is attached — both rankers predict per endpoint, and exactly one of them records per request (`candidates_for` with a policy, `best_group` without). Recording in both would double-count the winning group and pull the p95 toward the fastest one.
